books.section: Topic 7.7 1920s: Innovations in Communication and Technology

primary_sources: Ford Model T advertisement, LIFE magazine, October 1908

stimulus.text: The advertisement, from LIFE magazine, October 1908, shows an open five-passenger touring car at the top. Its headline reads: “The Ford Four Cylinder, Twenty Horse Power, Five Passenger Touring Car $850.00 Fob. Detroit.” Above the headline it says: “HIGH PRICED QUALITY IN A LOW PRICED CAR.” At the bottom: “Ford Motor Company, Detroit.”
stimulus.source_note: Ford Model T advertisement, LIFE magazine, October 1908, via The Henry Ford (Flickr), CC BY-SA 2.0. The headline and price are the advertiser's own wording.

source: original; stimulus image from the shared pool, Ford Model T advertisement, LIFE magazine, October 1908, CC BY-SA 2.0
stem: By the 1920s, the sales approach shown in this 1908 advertisement had become

options.text: rare, as cars grew too costly to buy
options.misconception: Cars grew cheaper, not costlier, as the line spread. By 1925 a touring car cost 290 dollars, down from 850 dollars in 1908.

options.text: illegal, since Congress banned all car advertising
options.misconception: Congress never banned car advertising. Advertising grew through the 1920s and became a major industry.

options.text: common, as mass-produced goods reached ordinary buyers
pointless, since Americans had stopped buying cars
options.misconception: Americans bought more cars, not fewer. Registrations rose from about 9 million in 1920 to nearly 27 million in 1930.

rationales.A: Cars grew cheaper, not costlier, as the line spread. By 1925 a touring car cost 290 dollars, down from 850 dollars in 1908.
rationales.B: Congress never banned car advertising. Advertising grew through the 1920s and became a major industry.
rationales.C: Background: by the late 1920s, about 23 million cars were on American roads, and most were bought on credit. Ads like this one had taught ordinary buyers to want mass-produced goods.
rationales.D: Americans bought more cars, not fewer. Registrations rose from about 9 million in 1920 to nearly 27 million in 1930.
rationales.general:
1. Note the date: the ad is from 1908, before the assembly line cut prices.
2. Follow the price: the same car cost 290 dollars by 1925, so ordinary buyers could afford it.
3. Name the result: selling quality at a low price became the normal pitch of the decade.
Remember: an early ad can show a method that only later becomes common.
